Pair
pâr
n. (two of a kind reckoned together; in Scripture, of shoes, turtledoves and balances — Greek zugos)
Latin par, equal, through Old French paire. The Greek zugos in Revelation 6:5 is a yoke or beam — a pair of balances is a yoke with a scale hung at either end.

Biblical Definition

Pair is a small word, and Scripture uses it at three heavy moments. Amos twice indicts Israel for the price at which men were sold: “because they sold the righteous for silver, and the poor for a pair of shoes” (Amo 2:6), and “That we may buy the poor for silver, and the needy for a pair of shoes; yea, and sell the refuse of the wheat?” (Amo 8:6). A man's freedom bartered for footwear — the prophet names the exchange rate to expose the contempt. Luke records the offering brought for the infant Christ: “And to offer a sacrifice according to that which is said in the law of the Lord, A pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons” (Luk 2:24). That was the concession Leviticus made for those who could not afford a lamb, and it tells us the household into which the Son of God was born. Revelation puts the word in the hand of the third horseman: “lo a black horse; and he that sat on him had a pair of balances in his hand” (Rev 6:5), and the voice that follows prices wheat and barley at famine rates. The three uses hold together: the poor sold for a pair of shoes, the Saviour's mother offering the poor woman's pair of birds, and a pair of balances weighing out bread in judgment.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a pair as two things of a kind, similar in form, applied to like things used together; two of a sort; a couple.

expand to see more

PAIR, n. Two things of a kind, similar in form, applied to the same purpose, or suited to each other; as a pair of shoes, a pair of gloves.

2. Two of a sort; a couple; a brace; as a pair of turtledoves.

3. In arithmetic and commerce, two corresponding parts of an instrument; as a pair of balances.

BAL'ANCE, n. A pair of scales for weighing commodities; a beam suspended in the middle, with a scale at each end.

Key Scripture

Revelation 6:5 — "And when he had opened the third seal, I heard the third beast say, Come and see. And I beheld, and lo a black horse; and he that sat on him had a pair of balances in his hand."

Luke 2:24 — "And to offer a sacrifice according to that which is said in the law of the Lord, A pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons."

Amos 2:6 — "Thus saith the LORD; For three transgressions of Israel, and for four, I will not turn away the punishment thereof; because they sold the righteous for silver, and the poor for a pair of shoes;"

Amos 8:6 — "That we may buy the poor for silver, and the needy for a pair of shoes; yea, and sell the refuse of the wheat?"

Modern Corruption

Poverty is treated as evidence of God's displeasure, when the law made a poor man's offering acceptable and the Lord of glory was presented with it.

expand to see more

Luke 2:24 settles a great deal by a small detail. Leviticus 12 required a lamb for a burnt offering and a young pigeon for a sin offering, and then made a provision: if she be not able to bring a lamb, then she shall bring two turtles or two young pigeons. Mary brought the pair of birds. The mother of the Lord came under the poverty clause of the law, and the offering was received without the smallest hint of deficiency. That is the standing answer to every doctrine that reads wealth as favour and want as judgment, and it is the answer God gave first by arranging the circumstances of His own Son's infancy.

Amos supplies the other half. God did not overlook what was being done to the poor of Israel, and the phrase He fastened on was the price: the poor for a pair of shoes. What the prophet exposes is not merely injustice but contempt — men bartered as cheaply as footwear, and the refuse of the wheat sold to them afterward. Wherever a system prices human beings so, Amos 2:6 is the verdict already pronounced. And the third seal keeps the accounting: a pair of balances in the hand of the rider, weighing out a day's wage for a day's wheat, so that men who dealt in false balances are finally weighed in a true one.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek zeugos (G2201), a yoke, a pair — Luke 2:24, Luke 14:19; zugos (G2218), a yoke or beam of a balance — Revelation 6:5; Hebrew naal (H5275), a sandal or pair of shoes.

expand to see more

Greek zeugos (G2201) — a pair, a yoke of animals; Luke 2:24 of the turtledoves, Luke 14:19 of five yoke of oxen.

Greek zugos (G2218) — a yoke, and the beam of a balance; Revelation 6:5, Matthew 11:29 of His easy yoke.

Hebrew naal (H5275) — a sandal; Amos 2:6 and 8:6, the price at which the poor were sold.

Leviticus 12:8 makes the pair of birds the offering of the woman who cannot afford a lamb.

Proverbs 11:1 sets the standard the third seal enforces: a false balance is abomination to the LORD.

Usage

"“The poor for a pair of shoes” — the prophet names the exchange rate."

"“A pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons” — the poor woman's offering, brought for Christ."

"“A pair of balances in his hand” — false weights answered by a true one."
